"The first is a name-and-arms clause, which is what my house is currently held under and which I would not recommend to anyone. It is a blunt instrument. The second is an entail, which is a Crown-registered instrument that fixes an estate to a specific line of descent and forbids it from passing to anyone outside that line, by marriage, adoption, or inheritance. Entails are old, they are expensive to register, and they are very hard to break. The Crown keeps a copy. That is the point of them."

She tapped the table once, twice.

"The third is what the Compact calls a separation of arms. It is not a single document. It is a set of provisions written into the marriage contract itself that say, in plain language, that neither house may absorb the other's titles, lands, or hereditary rights, and that if a single person becomes eligible to inherit both, the successions must be split before either is claimed. The Crown has upheld these provisions in every case that has come before it for two hundred years, because the Crown has no interest in seeing the great houses merge into three or four mega-houses it cannot balance against each other."

She looked at Ryan steadily.

"So the answer to your question is yes. All three instruments exist, and a competent advocate can draft them together. The entail is the one that actually protects Westcross across generations, because it is registered with the Crown and cannot be quietly reinterpreted by whoever is sitting in a parlor two hundred years from now. The separation of arms is the one that protects both houses from each other. I would want both. I would also want the marriage contract to name the entail as the controlling instrument if the two ever conflict, because in practice they can be read against each other by a clever advocate, and I have seen it done."
